title: Army band members and jazz for the French
summary: Most band members were from New Orleans; they played dance and jazz music, which French and American soldiers enjoyed.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Were there many from New Orleans in the band?

Quite a few. Quite a few of them, yes, from New Orleans. Because there's the trombone, two trombone players from New Orleans. Well, in fact, there were very few that wasn't. Because the piano players, the drummer, myself, and two cornet players, two trombone players, three clarinet players. Pretty much the whole thing was from New Orleans, those fellas. Only had two. That fella played piccolo and the guitar. They were small, so.
You don't recall any of those names?
Enos Hines, he's playing cornet, vice cornet, Andrew Barnett playing drums, Richard Biko playing bass, Richardson, piano player, I don't know his voice, can't think of his voice name.
Oh, I don't know.
And, uh, well, uh, William T. Bazile, he was playing get that, too.
Did you have to teach some of the people like you taught Jim Robinson?

Most of us. We started off with four. Four, and you had to teach them. Started out with four in Camp Pike. Had a lot of other fellas, good musicians. When we first went to camp, we used to come together some evening. But they split up. Went to different, uh, battalions. We had, uh, ours was 525th, they had 526th, 524th, 3rd, 4th, 5th, and 6th, 524th, like that. They just split up.
What kind of music did you play? From marching, or more like concerts for entertainment, you mentioned?

You mean that? No, it was a regular dance music. All, all kind of jazz. It was a brass band. Brass band, yes. That was, uh... Only very seldom we played two marches over there for two, who do the soldiers?
I see it says on the drum, jazz band.
Jazz band. That's all we had, jazz band.
I was going to ask, did the French people hear that, too? What did they think of that?
They hear that, too. They like it, too.
That was new for them, I guess,
wasn't it? You know, they kind of dance. That's their jazz, like that. They like that American jazz, too.
Was it new for the soldiers? Had they all heard that in this country, or was that sort of new for the soldiers, too, that kind of music?
Oh, the American soldiers? No, they wanted that. I mean, had they heard it before, that kind of music over here?
I guess it was mostly soldiers from the south.
Yes, sir. Well, maybe up north,
they hadn't heard that kind of music very much.
No, there's a lot of them, different camps we went to. We wish. Sometimes we'd go 150 miles.
Yeah.

Or put on a show, something like that. Well, they mixed in from the east and north, you know, some mixed in from the south up there. Well, then you, what you can tell when you get to a southern crew, though, and the Texas, too, they're like that. Yeah, you can tell when you hit that rock-bottom rhythm, too. They understood it. They understood it. They never get enough of it.
